author: Yasmine Johnson
title: Royal Commission puts pro-Palestine protesters on trial
content:
The Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion held a one-day hearing block on protests and policing on 4 August. Like the rest of the commission, it was more a prosecution than an inquiry: the Palestine solidarity movement was on trial, and its opponents were invited to act as judge, jury and witness.

The commission has already been filled with unsubstantiated and unchallenged testimony from so-called lived experience witnesses, often from pro-Israel lobby organisations. It is a platform for those wishing to slander the Palestine movement as antisemitic. In this hearing block, the fix was in from the beginning. Despite nearly three years of protests involving many thousands of people, the commission declared that just two protests would be discussed: a Sydney protest on 9 October 2023 that marched to the Opera House and a Nazi rally held by the National Socialist Network outside NSW Parliament on 8 November 2025.

The latter barely warranted a mention in the commission. It was fitting, given that one of the key, and outrageous, arguments pursued by pro-Israel organisations is that the left, rather than the far right, are the antisemites. This is in keeping with Israel’s alignment to extreme right-wing governments and parties around the world. author: James Plested
title: ‘Ready to fight for a socialist future’: eight hundred attend Victorian Socialists’ campaign launch
content:
It was the biggest event the Victorian Socialists (VS) have put on since we formed in 2018. On Saturday, 1 August, 800 people turned out to the Aborigines Advancement League in the northern Melbourne suburb of Thornbury to help us launch our campaign for the 2026 state election. Tickets were selling so fast in the week leading up to it that we had to scramble to ensure the bigger-than-expected crowd could be properly accommodated.

It’s a long time since the socialist movement in Australia has had to deal with an issue like this, and it was hard not to feel, on the night, that something significant has changed. The evening’s compere, VS candidate for Northcote Kath Larkin, expressed the feeling in her opening remarks. “We know that this election will not be easily won”, she said, “but if tonight is anything to go by, we’ve got masses of people who are ready to fight for a socialist future”.

For decades now the numbers of people concluding that the major problems in society are caused by capitalism, and that it’s socialist politics and organising that provide the answers, have never really gone beyond a slow drip. But watching the movement of hundreds of people up and down the steps leading into the central part of the launch venue evoked—in this hopeful mind at least—something like a waterfall. I’d have settled for a steady stream, but this felt like something more than that.

author: Alicia Griffiths
title: Melbourne tells Hanson where to go
content:
On the evening of 3 August, around 250 protesters gathered outside the Tower Hotel in Melbourne’s inner east. Inside, the far-right One Nation party was announcing its candidates for the Victorian state election to be held in November.

A large police presence was sent to protect the event and prevent protesters from getting near the venue. But our voices easily crossed the police lines, with the One Nation supporters being greeted with chants like, “Migrants are welcome, racists are not!” and “Pauline Hanson go to hell—take your racists there as well!” Party leader Pauline Hanson had slinked out through the adjoining bottle-o to avoid the protest.

The crowd heard speeches from a high school antifascist, a Swinburne student and a socialist involved in organising against Hanson when she first emerged as a political figure in the 1990s. The rally was called by the Campaign Against Racism and Fascism, which has been key to organising opposition to the far right in Melbourne over the last decade or more.

The protest was an important and much-needed display of opposition to Hanson, and something we will need more of in the lead-up to the state election. A campaign both in the streets and at the ballot box is needed to push back her racist, sexist, anti-worker agenda. author: Leon Whitehead
title: ‘Never again is now’: anti-fascist resistance in Germany
content:
GERMANY—On 4 July, the 100th anniversary of the Nazi Party’s second conference in the German state of Thuringia, the far-right Alternative for Germany (Alternative für Deutschland, AfD) held its federal party conference in a neighbouring city in the same state.

Putting the anti-fascist slogan “Never again is now” into practice, more than 17,000 anti-fascists blockaded every entrance to the venue, chanting “Hooray! Hooray! The Antifa is here today!”

Given the grim political climate in Germany, these protests are sorely needed. Increased military spending is leading to funding being stripped from health care, welfare, housing, youth clubs and museums. The postwar taboo—German rearmament—has been broken: Chancellor Friedrich Merz now speaks of making the German armed forces the “strongest conventional army in Europe”. His coalition government of the Christian Union and Social Democratic Party has taken the first step to reintroducing conscription for millions of young people.

Attacks on the working class are coming hard and fast: on 2 July, the government unveiled tax, pension and labour measures that included mandating a doctor’s note for all sick days and raising the retirement age to 70. The government also plans to extend the working day.

author: Mahee Hossain
title: Indian students shake Modi’s regime
content:
Earlier this month, more than 20,000 supporters cheered as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi stood triumphantly with his Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese at Melbourne’s Marvel Stadium. Modi, who has ruled India for more than twelve years, was repeatedly described by the press during his visit as the popular leader of the world’s largest democracy. By the end of the month, the actions of hundreds of thousands of angry students had forced the Modi regime to make concessions to the most significant mass movement in India in a long time.

Following dramatic wins in regional elections earlier in the year, including in the historically left-wing dominated state of West Bengal, Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP, Indian People’s Party) seemed stronger than ever. But the results papered over a growing crack of discontent, mainly among young people.

Young people have not benefited from the economic improvements Modi likes to tout. Among graduates aged under 30, 11 million out of 63 million are unemployed. In a now-infamous speech in May, India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, referred to these unemployed youth as “cockroaches” and “parasites” who would rather become activists than join the workforce. author: AEU members
title: Victorian teachers strike again
content:
At 1.44pm on 21 July, the news broke: Australian Education Union (AEU) members had once again voted to reject a substandard offer put to us by the state Labor government and our union leaders. It was a brilliant moment, even if at the time I was in class and not with my colleagues. Students eating their lunch wondered why I suddenly looked so thrilled. “The strike’s on!” I shouted, and they erupted into chanting, “Strike! Strike! Strike! Strike!”

While we could all agree that another day off school was something to be excited about, the significance of the win goes far deeper. This was the second time that AEU members have been asked to vote on an offer that failed to address our key demands, and the second time members said, “No, thanks, let’s keep fighting”. 

The strike later that week was an incredible display of resistance and solidarity, tens of thousands walking off the job for the second time this year. Given the AEU has called only one strike in the last thirteen years, it represented a significant achievement. The strong vote in favour of rejecting the second agreement and fighting for more was not only a win against the industrial action-averse union leadership, but also against the Labor government, which has continually undervalued our work and underestimated our resolve. The strong attendance at the rally was a testament to the commitment of teachers to win a bet

author: Danica Rachel
title: More strikes on the table after Pilbara drought broken
content:
An eight-hour strike on 16 July in Port Hedland, Western Australia, has broken a decades-long drought in the Pilbara iron ore industry. About 100 workers at BHP’s port downed tools, including members of the Electrical Trades Union (ETU), Australian Manufacturing Workers’ Union, and the Western Mineworkers’ Alliance.

It was the first strike at BHP since January 2000, and the first in the region’s iron ore industry since 2008. It represents a significant milestone towards rebuilding union power in what used to be a stronghold of workers’ militancy.

The strikers are staring down unrelenting pressure from the company and its friends in the capitalist press. In the lead-up, the pages of the 

West Australian

 warned of “chaos” and millions of dollars supposedly to be lost from the state budget. Afterwards, it gloated about how apparently little the strike had really mattered.

True, there was still iron ore shipped out during the strike. But it was still a major event. And despite the 

West

’s spin that the turnout was “dismal”, ETU state Secretary Adam Woodage confirmed that every electrician walked off the site.

author: Ruby Healer
title: Hanson is hardening up a far-right base—we need to organise against her
content:
When Marine Le Pen stepped in to replace her Holocaust-denying father as leader of the French National Front in 2011, it was part of a strategy to cleanse the far-right party of associations with Nazism. Le Pen judged that distancing herself from overt racism was the only practical route to electability. The French dubbed this manoeuvre 

dédiabolisation

 (“de-demonisation”).

Fifteen years later, Australia’s homegrown far right is moving in exactly the opposite direction. Pauline Hanson—a creature who initially slithered out of the Australian conservative tradition as a Liberal candidate in 1996—now openly calls for cultural homogenisation and actively seeks out the company of prominent neo-Nazis.

Hanson is making no attempt to sanitise her politics for the sake of broad appeal. On the contrary, she is hardening her political positions, becoming more unapologetically fascistic, and encouraging her supporters to follow.  

If anything, the more “official” endorsement Hanson receives—by way of National Press Club invitations, 

corporate donations

 and ex-Liberal backing—the more brazenly she pushes her extremist agenda. Political commentators are baffled by her apparent inability to judge what might hurt or help her “broad appeal”, but they misunderstand.

author: James Plested
title: Victorian Socialists to launch its biggest campaign yet
content:
The Victorian state election will be held on Saturday, 28 November. To date, most of the coverage of the election has been focused on the rise of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. If, as predicted, the party gains a breakthrough vote—perhaps even enough to strong-arm its way into a coalition government with the Liberals—it will be big news. One Nation would likely cement its spot as a genuine third force in mainstream politics and gain further momentum to take it through to the NSW state election in March 2027 and the next federal election, due by May 2028.

In the face of this, the increasingly unpopular Labor government is preparing to wage a classic, US Democrat-style “lesser evil” campaign—arguing that everyone who opposes One Nation must vote for Labor as the least-worst option among prospective parties of government. 

We’ve seen in country after country, though, that attempts by traditionally dominant capitalist parties to head off the threat posed by the far right by doubling down on the neoliberal status quo have only added fuel to the fire. Parties like Labor are incapable of pushing back the far right for the simple reason that they don’t offer anything that will improve the lives of working-class people and address the anger many feel.

author: Jasmine Duff
title: Royal commission: Israel supporters rationalise child killings, denounce critics as racist
content:
The universities block of the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion is over. One of the key throughlines in the testimonies of students, lobby groups and vice-chancellors was that criticism of Israel is antisemitic. The first day ended with a witness claiming that the murder of Palestinian children was a matter of “tough decisions”. Not a single Palestinian was given the opportunity to respond, and only two supporters of Palestine were allowed to speak: Yasmine Johnson and Dennis Altman. Both were allowed to testify only because they are Jewish.

The argument of many witnesses was straightforward: because most Jewish people are Zionists (supporters of the state of Israel), Zionism itself is a key part of Jewish identity, rather than simply a political ideology. Indeed, Commissioner Virginia Bell interrupted proceedings at one point to query Students for Palestine representative Yasmine Johnson’s Jewish identity, asking three questions:

“Did you grow up in a family that identified strongly as Jewish?”

“Do you have relatives who live in Israel?”

“When you were growing up, did you have an attachment to Israel in the sense of feeling some strong identification with Israel as the nation state of the Jews?”

author: Luca Tavan
title: Melbourne vice-chancellor undermines his own attempt to slander the Palestine movement
content:
There isn’t much space set aside for the truth at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. You have to really look for it, buried in day after day of spurious testimony by prejudiced witnesses who have little interest in the facts.

Sometimes a little bit of the truth slips out, though, as in this week’s testimony from the acting University of Melbourne vice-chancellor Glyn Davis. Davis’s own account inadvertently undermined the widespread establishment narrative that Palestine solidarity activism unleashed a torrent of antisemitism on the campuses.

The University of Melbourne Gaza solidarity encampment in 2024 was one of the most high-profile of the national wave of encampments that provoked a backlash from the political right and widespread media hysteria.

At the time, May 2024, deputy vice-chancellor Michael Wesley, who was tasked with addressing the media and issuing threats of discipline to the protesters, told Radio National that “there is antisemitism on campus”. He condemned the student occupation of the Arts West building as “intimidating” and said he could “only imagine how our students, particularly our Jewish students, would feel having to make their way to class through that”. University Council member Mark Leibler went further in an

Australian

article the same month, demanding recognition of a “crisis” of antisemitism on the campus.

author: D. Taylor
title: FROM THE VAULT: Zionist group admits making false accusation of antisemitism against student activists
content:
The following article was first published on 4 April 2016. The author, D. Taylor, is a Jewish socialist and at the time was leading Palestine solidarity activism at Monash University in Melbourne. We republish it today not only to show that there has always been a campaign of lies and slander, on the part of supporters of Israel, calling Palestine solidarity activists, even Jewish activists, antisemites. As Taylor wrote ten years ago:

[A]llegations of this nature, fabricated and promoted by “respectable” Zionist groups, are increasingly common. They are often repeated freely in the mainstream press and used as the basis for discipline on and off campus. The consequences for pro-Palestine activists can be devastating, which is precisely why the claims are made.

We republish it because the lies and slanders have become more brazen and unhinged as more and more people, particularly young people, have come to realise the true nature of the Israeli state and its crimes against the Palestinians.

4 APRIL 2016

—Australia’s largest pro-Israel student group has been caught making false allegations of antisemitism. It is not the first time that the Australasian Union of Jewish Students (AUJS) has done so. But, for once, it was caught lying and forced to issue a public retraction and apology to Socialist Alternative.

author: Alex McDouall
title: Brisbane protest stands against One Nation
content:
Loud cries of “Racist, sexist, anti-queer, Hanson is not welcome here!” resounded through the streets as more than 1,000 people marched against One Nation in Brisbane last weekend.

It was the first protest in Brisbane against Pauline Hanson since her recent rise in the polls. It was called in response to a transphobic rally supported by One Nation, at which Hanson was scheduled to speak—although she was replaced by her Senate colleague Malcolm Roberts. It was later reported that Hanson had travelled to the UK to schmooze with prominent fascist Tommy Robinson.

The protest was dominated by young people. High schoolers took to the streets alongside young workers. People came out of shops along the way to wave and show their support for the protest, some joining in. Many trans flags were waved throughout the crowd. So too were Palestinian flags and banners of the socialist left. This was not just a protest for trans rights; it was a protest against the inhumanity of the right and against all kinds of bigotry.

The police stopped us from getting close to the far-right demonstration, which attracted maybe 100 people.

author: Red Flag Radio
title: Fighting One Nation’s far-right insurgency
content:
The latest episode of Red Flag Radio is all about the breakthrough of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation Party. Chloe and Emma discuss why this far-right party has started polling upwards of 30 percent not by moderating their politics but by doubling down on all the fascist talking points of the global far right. Hanson’s Press Club speech was revealing: she railed against workers, migrants, trans people, mothers on parental leave and climate science. She called for Australia to become a “monoculture” and to “dig baby dig”.

They discuss some of the debates about how to respond to the rise of Hanson, from calls to understand the “legitimate concerns” of One Nation voters, to supporting the Labor Party come election time. They also talk about how the socialist left can get organised to take on Hanson and the system that created her.

author: Alexis Vassiley
title: Pilbara workers prepare to shut down BHP ports in historic strike
content:
Workers at BHP’s ports in Port Hedland, in Western Australia’s Pilbara, will down tools for eight hours tomorrow. Around 200 electricians, boilermakers, fitters and shiploaders will strike from 2pm to 10pm. Iron ore will not be loaded. The ports will grind to a halt. They will reportedly cost the largest company on the Australian stock exchange $50 million.

If this kind of strike action is unusual today, it’s even rarer in the Pilbara iron ore industry. This will be the first legal industrial action since Rio Tinto train drivers struck a handful of times in 2008. At BHP, the last time was a series of short strikes in December 1999 and January 2000, after union power had been smashed and individual contracts introduced.

Throughout the Pilbara iron ore industry, most workers are on above-award individual contracts (BHP and Rio Tinto train drivers are an exception). This means that their regular pay, yearly increase and any bonuses are pretty much completely determined by management. Two workers working side by side can be paid differently—to the tune of tens of thousands of dollars a year.

Management can also—and does—change crucial conditions, such as sick leave or rosters, as it sees fit. According to unions, BHP is proposing a “minimum rates agreement” that keeps these fundamentals intact. Essentially, this would be an enterprise agreement in name only.

author: Red Flag Staff
title: The socialist who schooled the royal commission
content:
The university block of Australia’s Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion is designed to provide a platform for pro-Israel students to denounce the Palestine solidarity movement on Australian university campuses. 

So lawyers at the commission thought they were going to “gotcha” Yasmine Johnson, a Jewish student, socialist and one of the national coordinators of Students for Palestine. But by remaining steadfast, she made them look foolish. Her written testimony noted:

My family history is part of what has compelled me to join and stay involved with the fight for Palestine, alongside a general progressive belief in a world without genocide, apartheid and ethnic cleansing. I’m appalled by the idea that the atrocities of the Holocaust—the systematic annihilation of Jewish lives which left my grandmother, like so many others, without remaining family—justify any of Israel’s current actions. The legacy of the historic injustices perpetrated against Jews, the mark of which has been left on my family, has strengthened my resolve to oppose genocide wherever it takes place.

author: Sarah Garnham
title: The day the royal commission got schooled by a Palestine solidarity activist
content:
Anyone with an ounce of humanity and a pinch of political sense can see that the current Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion is a farce. It is an open secret that it is a show trial of the Palestine movement. It is an echo chamber for some of Australia’s most ardent defenders of war crimes and genocide to talk about their hurt feelings. It is a fig leaf for the escalating assault on civil liberties and democratic rights.

Given all this, it was surprising that Yasmine Johnson, co-convenor of Students for Palestine and a member of Socialist Alternative, was accepted as a witness after almost all applications from Palestine solidarity groups to appear were denied. As one sympathetic supporter said on social media, “it was like matter meeting antimatter”.

The centrepiece of Yasmine’s testimony was that the Gaza genocide matters and that Palestinian lives matter more than the feelings of those who support their extermination (a word used by the United Nations Human Rights Commission to describe just one of Israel’s crimes against humanity). content:

Nevertheless, Students for Palestine—an activist group with chapters across the country, which led the student solidarity campaign—applied to appear before the commission to challenge some of the lies in an official and public setting.

author: Jasmine Duff
title: Responding to the lies against the student Palestine solidarity movement
content:
Every progressive movement and cause, at some stage, is slandered by its opponents. But the scale and extremity of the lies told to justify Israel’s genocide in Gaza are breathtaking. Most people who have become sympathetic to the Palestinian cause have been stunned by the slanders levelled against them by the political and media establishments. Opposition to war, genocide and racism has been painted at every step as racist and genocidal in intent.

These lies are used not only to portray Israel’s genocide as defensive and defensible, but also to justify serious attacks upon democratic rights and civil liberties in Australia. Since 2023, the federal Labor government has brought in successive laws and amendments that extend the extraordinarily repressive measures introduced during the “war on terror” and broadened the remit of Australia’s legislative anti-terror framework to include “hate speech” and groups deemed “hateful”. 

The project of establishing Israel, a Jewish supremacist ethno-state constructed on the historic lands of Palestine, has always been built upon lies. The first lie, told by a series of prominent figures in the early twentieth century, such as Ze’ev Jabotinsky, was that Palestine was “a land without a people”.
